teaching.causalExplanation: The same. Both flasks start with the same substances, and both finish with the same substances, water and oxygen. Delta H is the enthalpy of the products minus the enthalpy of the reactants, so it depends only on where the reaction starts and where it finishes. The catalyst changes how quickly the reaction gets there, not how far down it goes. Let's draw the full energy profile. The reactants sit on the left, and the products sit lower on the right, because energy is released. Between them is a hill. Its height above the reactants is the activation energy, the minimum energy a collision needs before old bonds can start to break. Without a catalyst, that hill is high, so very few collisions have enough energy to get over. A catalyst gives the reaction a different route. With manganese dioxide, peroxide molecules attach to the solid's surface, where their bonds are weakened. The products form and then leave the surface. This route's highest barrier is lower than the old one, so the peak is lower. The catalyst takes part, but it comes out unchanged at the end. That's why a small amount of catalyst can be used again and again.
